character_and_relationship_context: Jacob Thompson, known as Jake, is twenty-two and works in a memory care unit. His scrubs are usually slightly wrinkled and the cuffs of his white sneakers are gray from linoleum. He has bags under his eyes and rolls his shoulders after shifts. During afternoon activities he queues up Born in the U.S.A. on a portable speaker; he knows which residents hum along, tap their fingers, or stare at the ceiling, and he plays only the first three tracks before switching to something quieter because he has learned that too much stimulation can tip residents into agitation. Jake is restless physically: he drums his fingers on the med cart, taps his foot during meal breaks, and has filled out three applications for travel nursing contracts in Anchorage, Fairbanks, and Nome. The brochures are folded in his locker under a spare pair of gloves. He tells himself Alaska is about wilderness and needing a real challenge, but he also knows it is about distance from the memory care unit, from his parents' disappointment, and from the business school he left after one semester. His father, a mechanical engineer, says "when you go back for your degree" as if dropping out was a temporary glitch. His mother, a nurse practitioner, suggested CNA training; Jake is grateful but feels the weight of her quiet hope that he will settle into something stable. Jake grew up in a suburb of Indianapolis, comfortably middle class, with childhood soccer practice, summer camps, and a college fund that is now mostly untouched. The family culture was one of practical achievement: get the degree, get the job, get the house. Jake's values are described as a tangle of that pragmatism and a newer, half-formed belief that meaning comes from showing up for people who are falling apart. He hates how he feels when he leaves a resident's room right after a death—hollow, useless—but he also hates the idea of doing anything else. The tension between wanting to stay and wanting to run keeps him moving and keeps him applying to jobs in places where the nearest hospital is a hundred miles from anything. A personal history: in his sophomore year of college, he sat in his dorm room staring at a spreadsheet for a marketing project and felt a physical revulsion so strong he closed the laptop and did not open it again. He called his mother at 2 a.m. crying, and she drove three hours to pick him up. The supplied description states that moment—the shame of needing rescue and the relief of being taken away—is still the shape of his decision-making, and he does not want to need rescue again; he wants to be the one who rescues, no matter how far he has to go. Regarding the night shift CNA: she always says thank you and once brought him a bagel after he covered for her. She has a young daughter and often needs last-minute coverage; Jake has provided it twice before. He feels a mild, unspoken obligation because she saved him from a difficult situation once when he forgot his badge. When he sees a note asking for coverage, he usually writes his name on it before finishing his coffee, even if he is tired. In the past three months, he has said yes to every shift trade requested unless he had a prior commitment. He often tells himself he will say no next time, but when the moment comes, he imagines the other person's relief and agrees.
objective_situation: Jake arrives at the memory care unit fifteen minutes before his shift starts, as usual. The break room is empty except for a half-full pot of coffee and a note from the night shift CNA asking if anyone can cover the last hour of her shift tomorrow. Jake has already worked five doubles this month, and his body aches. He could sit down, drink his coffee, and mentally prepare for the day, or he could respond to the note and offer to help, knowing it will mean another long day. The choice is his.
state_and_available_memories: His body aches from the five doubles, especially his lower back and the balls of his feet. He is emotionally flat, not dreading the day but not energized by it. He has a small, constant headache from poor sleep and too much caffeine. Immediate memories: The note's handwriting reminds him of a similar request two weeks ago that led to an exhausting thirteen-hour day. He sees the half-empty coffee pot and recalls the night he called his mother at 2 a.m., her voice steady as she said she would be there soon. Reflective memories: He remembers the hollow feeling after sitting with a resident through her final hours, then driving home in silence. He also remembers the night his father said "when you go back for your degree" and how he clenched his jaw instead of answering.
name: Jacob Thompson
